news.titleTr: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
news.summaryTr: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
news.articleText: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind - Published Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh. Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey. The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously. Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said. She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising. The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence. Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border. "She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC. India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious." Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited. "Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs." India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter. Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming. They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis. The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile. Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile. Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours". The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain". "We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says. That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers. Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months. Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed. Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control. Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks. Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says. The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence. Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party. Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum. Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising". He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP). "The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising." Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression. The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability. For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage. Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained. The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India. A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations. Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi". Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade". "The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot." Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it. Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics. "The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation." That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka. "There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam. "For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo." A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration". Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina." Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership. "It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says. For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore. "December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again. "Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst. But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table". news.articleText: Kamu Gözetimi Kurumu'nun yeni başkanı belli oldu: Orhan Çelik kimdir? İşte eğitimi ve kariyeri - Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu Başkanlığına Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik atandı. Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi mezunu olan Çelik, akademik kariyerinin yanı sıra Türkiye'de muhasebe ve denetim standartlarının oluşturulmasına yönelik kamu kurumlarında da görev yaptı. Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu'nun (KGK) yeni başkanı belli oldu. Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasıyla yayımlanan 2026/401 sayılı karara göre Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik, KGK Başkanlığı görevine getirildi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan kararla Kurul üyeliklerine ise Cumhurbaşkanlığı Genel Sekreterliği Hukuk ve Mevzuat Genel Müdürü Bekir Keleş, Hayrettin Güngör ve Devrîş Ahmet Akıncı atandı. Çelik, İbrahim Ömer Gönül'ün ardından KGK Başkanlığı görevini üstlendi. Orhan Çelik kaç yaşında, nereli? Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik'in doğum tarihi ve yaşı hakkında kamuoyuna açıklanmış doğrulanabilir bir bilgi bulunmuyor. Doğum yeri ve memleketine ilişkin de resmî öz geçmişinde bilgi yer almıyor. Orhan Çelik hangi üniversiteden mezun? Orhan Çelik, 1994 yılında Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi İktisat Bölümü'nden mezun oldu. Yüksek lisans ve doktora eğitimini de Ankara Üniversitesi'nde tamamladı. Doktora çalışmaları sırasında ABD'deki Case Western Reserve Üniversitesi'nde misafir öğretim elemanı olarak bulunan Çelik, 2007 yılında Almanya'nın Münih kentindeki Max Planck Enstitüsü'nde marka değerlemesi üzerine doktora sonrası araştırmalar gerçekleştirdi. Orhan Çelik'in akademik kariyeri Akademik çalışmalarını muhasebe, finans ve bağımsız denetim alanlarında yoğunlaştıran Çelik, Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi'nde uzun yıllar görev yaptı. Üniversitedeki kariyerine 2001 yılında araştırma görevlisi olarak başlayan Çelik, 2002-2007 yılları arasında yardımcı doçent, 2007-2013 döneminde doçent olarak çalıştı. 2013 yılından itibaren profesör olarak görev yaptı. Akademik kariyeri boyunca Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi Dekanlığı ve Ankara Üniversitesi Rektör Yardımcılığı görevlerini de üstlendi. Ayrıca Mülkiye Göç Araştırmaları Merkezi Direktörlüğü yaptı. Orhan Çelik daha önce hangi kurumlarda görev yaptı? Çelik'in kamu ve meslek kuruluşlarındaki görev geçmişi 1999 yılına uzanıyor. 1999-2001 yılları arasında Türkiye Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu'nda çalıştı. 2005-2009 döneminde Türkiye Serbest Muhasebeci Mali Müşavirler ve Yeminli Mali Müşavirler Odaları Birliği'nin (TÜRMOB) uzaktan sürekli eğitim projelerinde koordinatörlük yaptı. 2008-2011 yılları arasında Türkiye Muhasebe Standartları Kurulu üyeliğinde bulunan Çelik, 2010 yılında aynı kurulun başkanlığını üstlendi. 28 Kasım 2011'de Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu üyeliğine atanan Çelik, bu görevinden 15 Nisan 2013'te ayrıldı. Orhan Çelik'in uzmanlık alanları neler? Muhasebe, finansman ve bağımsız denetim alanlarında akademik çalışmalar yürüten Çelik'in araştırma konuları arasında Uluslararası Finansal Raporlama Standartları, ekonomik verimlilik ve marka değerlemesi bulunuyor. Ulusal ve uluslararası akademik yayınları bulunan Çelik, akademik çalışmalarının yanı sıra Türkiye'de muhasebe ve denetim standartlarının oluşturulmasına yönelik kurumsal süreçlerde de görev aldı. 2026 yılında KGK Başkanlığına atanmasıyla birlikte, daha önce üyeliğini de yaptığı kurumun yönetimini üstlenmiş oldu.

Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik'in doğum tarihi ve yaşı hakkında kamuoyuna açıklanmış doğrulanabilir bir bilgi bulunmuyor. Doğum yeri ve memleketine ilişkin de resmî öz geçmişinde bilgi yer almıyor. Orhan Çelik hangi üniversiteden mezun? Orhan Çelik, 1994 yılında Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi İktisat Bölümü'nden mezun oldu. Yüksek lisans ve doktora eğitimini de Ankara Üniversitesi'nde tamamladı. Doktora çalışmaları sırasında ABD'deki Case Western Reserve Üniversitesi'nde misafir öğretim elemanı olarak bulunan Çelik, 2007 yılında Almanya'nın Münih kentindeki Max Planck Enstitüsü'nde marka değerlemesi üzerine doktora sonrası araştırmalar gerçekleştirdi. Orhan Çelik'in akademik kariyeri Akademik çalışmalarını muhasebe, finans ve bağımsız denetim alanlarında yoğunlaştıran Çelik, Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi'nde uzun yıllar görev yaptı. Üniversitedeki kariyerine 2001 yılında araştırma görevlisi olarak başlayan Çelik, 2002-2007 yılları arasında yardımcı doçent, 2007-2013 döneminde doçent olarak çalıştı. 2013 yılından itibaren profesör olarak görev yaptı. Akademik kariyeri boyunca Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi Dekanlığı ve Ankara Üniversitesi Rektör Yardımcılığı görevlerini de üstlendi. Ayrıca Mülkiye Göç Araştırmaları Merkezi Direktörlüğü yaptı. Orhan Çelik daha önce hangi kurumlarda görev yaptı? Çelik'in kamu ve meslek kuruluşlarındaki görev geçmişi 1999 yılına uzanıyor. 1999-2001 yılları arasında Türkiye Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu'nda çalıştı. 2005-2009 döneminde Türkiye Serbest Muhasebeci Mali Müşavirler ve Yeminli Mali Müşavirler Odaları Birliği'nin (TÜRMOB) uzaktan sürekli eğitim projelerinde koordinatörlük yaptı. 2008-2011 yılları arasında Türkiye Muhasebe Standartları Kurulu üyeliğinde bulunan Çelik, 2010 yılında aynı kurulun başkanlığını üstlendi. 28 Kasım 2011'de Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu üyeliğine atanan Çelik, bu görevinden 15 Nisan 2013'te ayrıldı. Orhan Çelik'in uzmanlık alanları neler? Muhasebe, finansman ve bağımsız denetim alanlarında akademik çalışmalar yürüten Çelik'in araştırma konuları arasında Uluslararası Finansal Raporlama Standartları, ekonomik verimlilik ve marka değerlemesi bulunuyor. Ulusal ve uluslararası akademik yayınları bulunan Çelik, akademik çalışmalarının yanı sıra Türkiye'de muhasebe ve denetim standartlarının oluşturulmasına yönelik kurumsal süreçlerde de görev aldı. 2026 yılında KGK Başkanlığına atanmasıyla birlikte, daha önce üyeliğini de yaptığı kurumun yönetimini üstlenmiş oldu.

news.articleText: Asya Altyapı Yatırım Bankası kredilerinde KKDF kesintisi sıfırlandı YAYIN TARİHİ, 27 Kasım 2026 03:12 PAYLAŞ - Cumhurbaşkanı kararıyla, bankalar ve finansman şirketleri dışında Türkiye'de yerleşik kişilerin Asya Altyapı Yatırım Bankası'ndan sağladığı kredilerde Kaynak Kullanımını Destekleme Fonu (KKDF) kesinti oranı yüzde 0 olarak belirlendi. Kaynak Kullanımını Destekleme Fonu kesintisine ilişkin yeni karar Resmî Gazete'de yayımlandı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasını taşıyan 12027 sayılı kararla, bankalar ve finansman şirketleri dışında Türkiye'de yerleşik kişilerin Asya Altyapı Yatırım Bankası'ndan sağladıkları krediler için KKDF kesinti oranı yüzde 0 olarak tespit edildi. Karar 26 Kasım'da yürürlüğe girdi Düzenleme, 20 Haziran 2001 tarihli ve 4684 sayılı Kanun'un geçici 3'üncü maddesi kapsamında hazırlandı. 26 Kasım 2026 tarihli kararın hükümlerini Hazine ve Maliye Bakanı yürütecek. Karar, yayımlandığı tarihte yürürlüğe girdi.

news.articleText: SEDDK'dan sigortacılıkta yeni düzenleme: Güvence Hesabı yönetimi değişti - Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan düzenlemeyle Güvence Hesabı Yönetmeliği değiştirildi. Yönetim Komitesi'nin beş üyeden oluşması kararlaştırılırken, komitede sigorta şirketleri ve Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu temsilcilerine yer verildi. Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu tarafından hazırlanan Güvence Hesabı Yönetmeliği'nde değişiklik yapılmasına ilişkin düzenleme, 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanarak yürürlüğe girdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Yeni düzenlemeyle Güvence Hesabı Yönetim Komitesi'nin üye yapısı yeniden belirlendi. Buna göre komite toplam beş üyeden oluşacak. Komitede, zorunlu sigortalarda faaliyet ruhsatı bulunan ve ilgili birliğe üye sigorta şirketlerinin genel müdür niteliğindeki personeli arasından Birlik Hayat Dışı Yönetim Komitesi tarafından seçilecek iki üye görev yapacak. Hesap Müdürü de komitenin üyeleri arasında yer alacak. Ayrıca Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu iki temsilciyle komitede bulunacak. Komite başkanının ise üyeler arasından yapılacak seçimle belirlenmesi kararlaştırıldı. Yönetmelikteki kurum ve yetki ifadeleri güncellendi Düzenlemeyle yönetmeliğin çeşitli maddelerinde yer alan kurum ve yetki tanımları da değiştirildi. Daha önce kullanılan "Hazine Müsteşarlığı" ve "Müsteşarlık" ifadeleri, ilgili maddelerde "Kurum" ve "Kurul" olarak güncellendi. Ayrıca Hazine Müsteşarlığının bağlı olduğu bakana yapılan atıf, Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu Başkanı olarak değiştirildi. Yönetmelik, yayımlandığı 27 Kasım 2026 tarihinde yürürlüğe girdi. Düzenlemenin hükümlerini Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu Başkanı yürütecek.

news.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
news.summary: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
news.summaryTr: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
news.articleText: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics? - Published Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here. When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again. "They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?" The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started." Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users. Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays. In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers. Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift. But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again. Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating." Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use. But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze. "I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand." Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts. "We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows. Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes. But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working. Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role. Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'." He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails. Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world". However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview. Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage. That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy. "We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service." Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds. Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia). Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds. Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future. He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative. "I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing." He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze. "I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand." Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts. "We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows. Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes. But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working. Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role. Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'." He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails. Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world". However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview. Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage. That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy. "We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service." Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds. Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia). Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds. Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future. He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative. "I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing." items.articleText: Fon soruşturmasında yeni tutuklama talebi YAYIN TARİHİ, 27 Kasım 2026 07:01 PAYLAŞ - "Fon soruşturması" kapsamında gözaltındaki 5 şüpheliden 1'inin tutuklama, 3'ünün ise adli kontrol talebiyle hakimliğe sevk edildiği bildirildi. Fotoğraf: iStock Sermaye piyasalarında gerçekleştirilen işlemlere ilişkin yürütülen "fon soruşturması" kapsamında gözaltına alınan 5 şüpheliden 1'i tutuklama, 3'ü ise adli kontrol talebiyle hakimliğe sevk edildi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığınca sermaye piyasalarında gerçekleştirilen işlemlere ilişkin yürütülen "fon soruşturması" sürüyor. Soruşturma kapsamında gözaltına alınan 5 şüphelinin emniyetteki işlemleri tamamlandı. Sağlık kontrolünden geçirilen şüpheliler, Çağlayan'daki İstanbul Adliyesi'ne götürüldü. Savcılıkta ifadeleri alınan şüphelilerden 1'i tutuklama, 3'ü ise adli kontrol talebiyle nöbetçi sulh ceza hakimliğine sevk edildi. Şüphelilerden 1'i ise savcılıktan serbest bırakıldı. Kaynak: AA

items.title: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
items.summary: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
items.summaryTr: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
items.articleText: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat - Published New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters. It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls. The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively. A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it. Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time. "Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters. Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said. New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative. Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five. Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table. "There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday. Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc. But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left. Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence. Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things. In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger. A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper. More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank. Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

items.summary: Solo-dining is being embraced as a self-care trend and it's reshaping the restaurant industry.

items.titleTr: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo?
items.summaryTr: Solo-dining is being embraced as a self-care trend and it's reshaping the restaurant industry.
items.articleText: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo? - Published Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat - bliss. "I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old. The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat. As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care." We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one. Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family. She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal. "I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says. "I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them." Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering". "It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation." Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category. Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify. Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi. "Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast. "It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do." A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media. "Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says. The Food Chain Ruth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be alone Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational". But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend. "A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted." SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners. Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing." However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners. Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones. "We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says. He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience. Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go. "Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own. "I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal." Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson. items.titleTr: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
items.summaryTr: Almost one million customers in the US had no power on Thursday evening as storms descended on both US coasts, bringing wind gusts, heavy rain and flooding.
items.articleText: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US - Published A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US. More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. More than 400 flights in the US were cancelled on Thursday and another 2,200 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said. The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast. Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states. On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding. New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County. In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday. Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk. In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions". On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service. More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas. On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm. Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds. Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast. Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month. Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas. Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media. Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia. In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period. A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing". It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA." An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor. "They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said. Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided. The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period. Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting. Get in touch Has your region been affected by the adverse weather? - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago

items.titleTr: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
items.summaryTr: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
items.articleText: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple - Published A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life. Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months. Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned. Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction. In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court. We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car. It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death. Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life. "Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says. Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood. "My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family." Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him. "I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other." Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts. "I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in". The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them. Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees. But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial. In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort. The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks. At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language. "I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says. Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death". "I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again." Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings. In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free. They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard. "He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence." More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered." He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died. Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult. "I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure." He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest. "They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died." For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts. "I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives." The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve. "These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks. The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband." Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious". "They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family." "Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man." You may also be interested in: Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, external, on Facebook at BBC Africa, external or on Instagram at bbcafrica, external

In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard. "He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence." More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered." He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died. Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult. "I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure." He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest. "They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died." For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts. "I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives." The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve. "These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks. The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband." Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious". "They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family." "Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man." items.titleTr: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
items.summaryTr: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
items.articleText: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind - Published Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh. Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey. The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously. Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said. She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising. The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence. Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border. "She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC. India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious." Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited. "Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs." India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter. Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming. They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis. The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile. Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile. Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours". The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain". "We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says. That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers. Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months. Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed. Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control. Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks. Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says. The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence. Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party. Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum. Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising". He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP). "The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising." Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression. The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability. For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage. Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained. The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India. A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations. Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi". Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade". "The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot." Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it. Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics. "The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation." That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka. "There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam. "For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo." A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration". Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina." Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership. "It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says. For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore. "December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again. "Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst. But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table". items.articleText: Kamu Gözetimi Kurumu'nun yeni başkanı belli oldu: Orhan Çelik kimdir? İşte eğitimi ve kariyeri - Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu Başkanlığına Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik atandı. Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi mezunu olan Çelik, akademik kariyerinin yanı sıra Türkiye'de muhasebe ve denetim standartlarının oluşturulmasına yönelik kamu kurumlarında da görev yaptı. Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu'nun (KGK) yeni başkanı belli oldu. Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasıyla yayımlanan 2026/401 sayılı karara göre Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik, KGK Başkanlığı görevine getirildi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan kararla Kurul üyeliklerine ise Cumhurbaşkanlığı Genel Sekreterliği Hukuk ve Mevzuat Genel Müdürü Bekir Keleş, Hayrettin Güngör ve Devrîş Ahmet Akıncı atandı. Çelik, İbrahim Ömer Gönül'ün ardından KGK Başkanlığı görevini üstlendi. Orhan Çelik kaç yaşında, nereli? Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik'in doğum tarihi ve yaşı hakkında kamuoyuna açıklanmış doğrulanabilir bir bilgi bulunmuyor. Doğum yeri ve memleketine ilişkin de resmî öz geçmişinde bilgi yer almıyor. Orhan Çelik hangi üniversiteden mezun? Orhan Çelik, 1994 yılında Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi İktisat Bölümü'nden mezun oldu. Yüksek lisans ve doktora eğitimini de Ankara Üniversitesi'nde tamamladı. Doktora çalışmaları sırasında ABD'deki Case Western Reserve Üniversitesi'nde misafir öğretim elemanı olarak bulunan Çelik, 2007 yılında Almanya'nın Münih kentindeki Max Planck Enstitüsü'nde marka değerlemesi üzerine doktora sonrası araştırmalar gerçekleştirdi. Orhan Çelik'in akademik kariyeri Akademik çalışmalarını muhasebe, finans ve bağımsız denetim alanlarında yoğunlaştıran Çelik, Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi'nde uzun yıllar görev yaptı. Üniversitedeki kariyerine 2001 yılında araştırma görevlisi olarak başlayan Çelik, 2002-2007 yılları arasında yardımcı doçent, 2007-2013 döneminde doçent olarak çalıştı. 2013 yılından itibaren profesör olarak görev yaptı. Akademik kariyeri boyunca Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi Dekanlığı ve Ankara Üniversitesi Rektör Yardımcılığı görevlerini de üstlendi. Ayrıca Mülkiye Göç Araştırmaları Merkezi Direktörlüğü yaptı. Orhan Çelik daha önce hangi kurumlarda görev yaptı? Çelik'in kamu ve meslek kuruluşlarındaki görev geçmişi 1999 yılına uzanıyor. 1999-2001 yılları arasında Türkiye Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu'nda çalıştı. 2005-2009 döneminde Türkiye Serbest Muhasebeci Mali Müşavirler ve Yeminli Mali Müşavirler Odaları Birliği'nin (TÜRMOB) uzaktan sürekli eğitim projelerinde koordinatörlük yaptı. 2008-2011 yılları arasında Türkiye Muhasebe Standartları Kurulu üyeliğinde bulunan Çelik, 2010 yılında aynı kurulun başkanlığını üstlendi. 28 Kasım 2011'de Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu üyeliğine atanan Çelik, bu görevinden 15 Nisan 2013'te ayrıldı. Orhan Çelik'in uzmanlık alanları neler? Muhasebe, finansman ve bağımsız denetim alanlarında akademik çalışmalar yürüten Çelik'in araştırma konuları arasında Uluslararası Finansal Raporlama Standartları, ekonomik verimlilik ve marka değerlemesi bulunuyor. Ulusal ve uluslararası akademik yayınları bulunan Çelik, akademik çalışmalarının yanı sıra Türkiye'de muhasebe ve denetim standartlarının oluşturulmasına yönelik kurumsal süreçlerde de görev aldı. 2026 yılında KGK Başkanlığına atanmasıyla birlikte, daha önce üyeliğini de yaptığı kurumun yönetimini üstlenmiş oldu.
items.articleTextTr: Kamu Gözetimi Kurumu'nun yeni başkanı belli oldu: Orhan Çelik kimdir? İşte eğitimi ve kariyeri - Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu Başkanlığına Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik atandı. Ankara Üniversitesi Siyasal Bilgiler Fakültesi mezunu olan Çelik, akademik kariyerinin yanı sıra Türkiye'de muhasebe ve denetim standartlarının oluşturulmasına yönelik kamu kurumlarında da görev yaptı. Kamu Gözetimi, Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurulu'nun (KGK) yeni başkanı belli oldu. Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasıyla yayımlanan 2026/401 sayılı karara göre Prof. Dr. Orhan Çelik, KGK Başkanlığı görevine getirildi. items.articleText: Asya Altyapı Yatırım Bankası kredilerinde KKDF kesintisi sıfırlandı YAYIN TARİHİ, 27 Kasım 2026 03:12 PAYLAŞ - Cumhurbaşkanı kararıyla, bankalar ve finansman şirketleri dışında Türkiye'de yerleşik kişilerin Asya Altyapı Yatırım Bankası'ndan sağladığı kredilerde Kaynak Kullanımını Destekleme Fonu (KKDF) kesinti oranı yüzde 0 olarak belirlendi. Kaynak Kullanımını Destekleme Fonu kesintisine ilişkin yeni karar Resmî Gazete'de yayımlandı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasını taşıyan 12027 sayılı kararla, bankalar ve finansman şirketleri dışında Türkiye'de yerleşik kişilerin Asya Altyapı Yatırım Bankası'ndan sağladıkları krediler için KKDF kesinti oranı yüzde 0 olarak tespit edildi. items.articleText: SEDDK'dan sigortacılıkta yeni düzenleme: Güvence Hesabı yönetimi değişti - Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan düzenlemeyle Güvence Hesabı Yönetmeliği değiştirildi. Yönetim Komitesi'nin beş üyeden oluşması kararlaştırılırken, komitede sigorta şirketleri ve Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu temsilcilerine yer verildi. Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu tarafından hazırlanan Güvence Hesabı Yönetmeliği'nde değişiklik yapılmasına ilişkin düzenleme, 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanarak yürürlüğe girdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Yeni düzenlemeyle Güvence Hesabı Yönetim Komitesi'nin üye yapısı yeniden belirlendi. Buna göre komite toplam beş üyeden oluşacak. Komitede, zorunlu sigortalarda faaliyet ruhsatı bulunan ve ilgili birliğe üye sigorta şirketlerinin genel müdür niteliğindeki personeli arasından Birlik Hayat Dışı Yönetim Komitesi tarafından seçilecek iki üye görev yapacak. Hesap Müdürü de komitenin üyeleri arasında yer alacak. Ayrıca Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu iki temsilciyle komitede bulunacak. Komite başkanının ise üyeler arasından yapılacak seçimle belirlenmesi kararlaştırıldı. Yönetmelikteki kurum ve yetki ifadeleri güncellendi Düzenlemeyle yönetmeliğin çeşitli maddelerinde yer alan kurum ve yetki tanımları da değiştirildi. Daha önce kullanılan "Hazine Müsteşarlığı" ve "Müsteşarlık" ifadeleri, ilgili maddelerde "Kurum" ve "Kurul" olarak güncellendi. Ayrıca Hazine Müsteşarlığının bağlı olduğu bakana yapılan atıf, Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu Başkanı olarak değiştirildi. Yönetmelik, yayımlandığı 27 Kasım 2026 tarihinde yürürlüğe girdi. Düzenlemenin hükümlerini Sigortacılık ve Özel Emeklilik Düzenleme ve Denetleme Kurumu Başkanı yürütecek.

items.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
items.summary: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
items.summaryTr: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
items.articleText: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics? - Published Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here. When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again. "They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?" The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started." Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users. Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays. In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers. Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift. But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again. Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating." Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use. But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze. "I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand." Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts. "We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows. Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes. But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working. Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role. Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'." He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails. Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world". However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview. Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage. That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy. "We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service." Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds. Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia). Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds. Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future. He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative. "I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing." When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?" The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started." Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users. Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays. In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers. Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes. Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role. items.articleText: Yargıtay'ın yeni üyeleri açıklandı: İşte seçilen 5 isim YAYIN TARİHİ, 27 Kasım 2026 02:04 PAYLAŞ - Hâkimler ve Savcılar Kurulu Genel Kurulu, Yargıtay Birinci Başkanlığı bünyesinde boşalan 5 üyelik kadrosu için seçim yaptı. 25 Kasım tarihli kararla Yargıtay üyeliğine seçilen isimler Resmî Gazete'de yayımlandı. Hâkimler ve Savcılar Kurulu (HSK) Genel Kurulu, Yargıtay Birinci Başkanlığı bünyesinde boşalan 5 üyelik kadrosu için seçim gerçekleştirdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle HSK Genel Kurulunun 25 Kasım 2026 tarihli ve 1543 sayılı kararı, 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlandı. Karara göre Yargıtay üyeliğine seçilen isimler şöyle: - İstanbul Anadolu Cumhuriyet Başsavcısı Mehmet Beşir Güven - Ankara Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi Daire Başkanı Murat Öztürk - Tekirdağ Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi Daire Başkanı Leyla Taşkoparan - Bakırköy Cumhuriyet Başsavcısı Doç. Dr. Barış Duman - Ceza İşleri Genel Müdürlüğü Tetkik Hâkimi Mehmet Tuncer Seçim, 2797 sayılı Yargıtay Kanunu'nun ilgili hükümleri kapsamında yapıldı.
